blocks.stage: LANGUAGE · the argument move set
blocks.title: <ico-book></ico-book> CLAIM, CONCEDE, REBUT
blocks.intro: A debate is not a fight. It is a set of moves: make a claim, back it up, give the other side what is true, and then turn. Five moves, and the phrases that signal each one.

vocab.sp: the statement that the two sides argue about
to give reasons to support or oppose something
the idea an argument is built on
to admit that the other side is right about one thing
to answer an argument and show why it is weak
to keep speaking; to have the right to speak
the person who runs the debate
your last, short summary of your case

blocks.note: How it works: flashcards , listening , a dialogue where you take a seat in the debate, gap-fill , compare and order . Press CHECK wherever you see it.

parts.html: 1 · CLAIM, EVIDENCE, SO WHAT — an opinion with nothing behind it is only an opinion

items.en: Closing the center to cars would make this city healthier.
items.sp: The claim: one sentence, no hedging.

items.en: In cities that have done it, air pollution has fallen by a third.
items.sp: The evidence: a number, a case, an example.

items.en: So this isn't about comfort. It's about health.
items.sp: The «so what»: why the evidence matters.

parts.html: 2 · CONCEDE, THEN TURN — give them what is true, and keep your ground

items.en: Granted, deliveries would be harder; however, they can be scheduled.
That's a fair point, but it overlooks the people who live there.
items.sp: A fair point = I accept it. It overlooks = it forgets something.

parts.html: 3 · ATTACK THE ARGUMENT, NOT THE PERSON

items.en: I'd challenge the premise that stores need parking.
items.sp: You question the idea underneath the argument.

items.en: With respect, the evidence points the other way.
items.sp: You disagree with the evidence, not with the speaker.

parts.body: You clearly don't understand business. → I'd challenge the premise that this is bad for business. The first one loses the audience, even if you are right.

parts.html: 4 · HEDGE THE WEAK, BOOST THE STRONG — be exactly as sure as your evidence

items.en: Arguably, the plan would help small stores.
items.sp: Hedge: I can argue it, but I can't prove it.

items.en: The evidence suggests that sales would rise.
Undoubtedly, the air would be cleaner.
items.sp: Boost: nobody can reasonably deny it.

parts.html: 5 · FLOOR MANAGEMENT — keep it, take it, give it back

items.en: If I could just finish my point.
items.sp: Keep the floor: firm, never angry.
Take the floor: you ask before you interrupt.

items.en: Let me pick up on that.
items.sp: Take the floor by building on what was said.

parts.html: SPANISH TRAP — cinco errores que se oyen en cualquier debate

items.sp: Agree ya es verbo: nunca I am agree.

items.en: We discussed the plan. Then they argued about money.
She is very sensible: she always plans ahead.

items.sp: Argument es un razonamiento, además de una pelea.

parts.body: I am agree. → I agree. · It depends of the price. → It depends on the price.

blocks.title: <ico-star></ico-star> DEBATE NIGHT
blocks.intro:
Once a month, The Signal hands the studio over to an argument. Tonight's motion: «This city should close its center to cars.» Priya argues for, Max against, and Nora keeps the peace. Your job: time the speakers and note every move.

WORDS OF THE DAY (they must appear in your writing): a premise = the idea an argument stands on · sit on the fence · concede a point.

cast.sp: argues for: she runs a tech team downtown
argues against: he owns a furniture store

blocks.title: THE MOVE PHRASES · tap to flip
blocks.intro: Ten phrases, each one a move. Before you flip, say which move it is: concede, rebut, hedge, boost, or manage the floor.

cards.back: concede, then turn · «Granted, it's expensive; however, it works.»
concede, then turn · «That's a fair point, but it isn't the whole story.»
rebut: something was forgotten · «It overlooks the people who live there.»
rebut: question the idea underneath · «I'd challenge the premise that cars bring customers.»
hedge: it can be argued, not proved · «Arguably, it's the best plan we have.»
hedge with data · «The evidence suggests that sales rise.»
boost: nobody can deny it · «Undoubtedly, the air would be cleaner.»
keep the floor · «If I could just finish my point, Max.»
take the floor politely · «Can I come in here? I have the numbers.»

cards.front: Let me pick up on that.
cards.back: take the floor by building on the last point · «Let me pick up on that, because it matters.»

blocks.title: AUDIO 1 · THE DEBATE
blocks.desc: Priya and Max on the motion, with Nora in the chair. Each of them makes a claim, gives evidence, concedes one point and rebuts another. There is one interruption: listen to how it is handled.

options: His sales fell by forty percent when his street was closed for repairs
Air pollution fell by a third in three cities
People on foot stay longer and spend more
That cleaner air is not a priority
That stores selling large items would need a different solution

questions.q: Which phrase does Priya use to take the floor back?
options: If I could just finish my point

questions.q: What has happened to Max's position by the end?
options: It has softened: he could accept the plan if store owners are consulted first
It has hardened: he now rejects any change

speaking.prompt: You are the next speaker. Concede one point to Max and then turn it, in two sentences.
speaking.starter: Granted, (Max's point); however, (your point). / That's a fair point, but it overlooks (what).

transcript.html: Welcome to Debate Night on The Signal. Tonight's motion: "This city should close its center to cars." Arguing for, Priya, who runs a technology team downtown. Arguing against, Max, who owns a furniture store on Main Street. Priya, you have the floor.

Thank you, Nora. My claim is simple: closing the center to cars would make this city healthier and richer. Here is the evidence. In the three cities of our size that have done it, air pollution in the center fell by a third within two years. And people on foot stay longer and spend more. So this isn't about hating cars. It's about what a center is for.

Undoubtedly, cleaner air is a good thing. Nobody is arguing for pollution. But I'd challenge the premise that people on foot spend more in every kind of store. I sell sofas. Nobody carries a sofa home on a bicycle. Last year, when my street was closed for six weeks of repairs, my sales fell by forty percent. That's not a theory. That's my accounts.

That's a fair point, Max, and I won't pretend otherwise: stores that sell large items would need a different solution. But it overlooks one thing. Your street was closed for repairs, with noise and dust and no plan. That's not the same as
It's exactly the same for my customers. They couldn't park, so they
If I could just finish my point, Max. A construction site is not a pedestrian street. In the cities I mentioned, delivery vans are allowed in before ten a.m., and stores like yours deliver for free.
Max, would that change your mind?
Granted, morning deliveries would help. However, somebody has to pay for free delivery, and arguably it would be small stores like mine.
We're almost out of time. One sentence each, please.
The evidence suggests that centers without cars do better, so let's solve the delivery problem instead of keeping the traffic.
Close the center if you must, but not before you've asked the people who work there.
Thank you both. Listeners, the lines are open.

blocks.title: TAKE MAX'S SEAT
blocks.intro: You argue against the motion; Priya argues for it. Choose the reply that concedes and then turns. The other two either attack the person or give up the point.

lines.html: Cities without cars in the center are simply better places to live.

options: You only say that because you don't own a store.
That may be true for residents. But I'd challenge the premise that it's better for every business.
You're probably right. I have nothing to add.

lines.html: Air pollution fell by a third in three cities.

options: Granted, the air improved. However, those cities had better public transportation than we do.
Well, if the numbers say so, I give up.

lines.html: People on foot stay longer and spend more.

options: You've clearly never worked in a store.
I suppose that's the end of my argument, then.
That's a fair point for cafés, but it overlooks stores that sell heavy goods.

lines.html: Vans can deliver before ten in the morning.

options: Arguably, that would help. Even so, somebody has to pay for it.
That's a ridiculous idea, like all your ideas.

lines.html: But you're ignoring the people who

options: Stop interrupting me! It's so rude.
If I could just finish, Priya. I'm almost done.
Sorry, sorry. Go ahead. I'll stop.

blocks.title: HEDGE OR BOOST?
blocks.intro: How sure can you be? Choose the word that matches the strength of the evidence, and watch the Spanish traps.

items.q: ___, cleaner air is a good thing. Nobody disagrees with that.
___, the plan would help small stores, though nobody can prove it yet.
We only have two studies, but the evidence ___ that people on foot spend more.
I ___ with you on that point.
That's a fair point, but it ___ the people who live there.
I'd challenge the ___ that stores need parking.
___, deliveries would be harder; however, they can be scheduled.

blocks.title: YOU'RE WRONG vs I'D CHALLENGE THAT
blocks.intro: Both say «I disagree». One ends the conversation; the other continues it.

items.q: Which one goes after the idea, not the person?
Which one is likely to make the other person stop listening?
What does "I'd" (I would) do in B?
options: It puts the sentence in the past
It makes the speaker sound unsure of the facts
It softens the move: firm, but not an insult

items.q: Your opponent makes a good point. Which reply keeps you in the debate?
options: That's a fair point, but it overlooks the cost.
That's a fair point. I was wrong about everything.
I am agree with you up to a point.
I agree with you up to a point.
I agree to you up to a point.

blocks.title: AUDIO 2 · THE VOICEMAILS
blocks.desc: After the debate, three listeners call in: Sam, Kit and Robin. Each one has twenty seconds. Who agrees with the motion, who disagrees, and who sits on the fence?

questions.q: Where does Sam stand on the motion?
Which caller raises a point that neither debater mentioned?
Which phrase tells you that Robin has not chosen a side?

speaking.prompt: Leave your own twenty-second voicemail on the motion. Start by conceding one point to the other side.
speaking.starter: Hi, this is (name). Granted, (the other side's point). However, (your position), because (your reason).

transcript.html: Hi, this is Sam, the baker from a few weeks ago. I'm with Priya on this one. My bread goes out before six in the morning anyway, so the delivery rule wouldn't hurt me at all. And honestly, I'd love customers who aren't in a hurry to get back to their cars. Close it. I'm in.

Hello, Kit here. I have to disagree. My mother is eighty-two, and she can't walk more than a block. If I can't drive her to her doctor downtown, she simply doesn't go. Nobody mentioned people like her tonight. Until they do, my answer is no.

Hi, it's Robin. Honestly, I can see both sides. Priya's numbers are impressive. That said, Max knows his own street better than any study does. I'd want to see a three-month trial before I decide. Sorry. I know that's not much of an answer.

blocks.title: <ico-pen></ico-pen> MY CLOSING STATEMENT
blocks.intro: The debate is ending and you have one minute. Write your closing statement for or against the motion «This city should close its center to cars» (about 120 words).
checklist: One piece of evidence (a number, a case, an example), with a hedge or a booster that fits it
One concession to the other side (Granted,… / That's a fair point, but…)
One rebuttal that goes after the idea, not the person (I'd challenge the premise that… / It overlooks…)
A last line people will remember, and the words of the day
blocks.placeholder: Tonight we have heard two views of this city…
blocks.example: your claim. Undoubtedly / Arguably / The evidence suggests that evidence. Granted, the other side's best point; however, your answer. I'd challenge the premise that the idea you reject. last line.
blocks.hw: Write your statement, then record it in under one minute, standing up, as if the audience were in front of you. Send me the text and the audio on WhatsApp.

rubric.d: About 120 words, clearly for or against, with claim, evidence, concession, rebuttal and close.
The concession really gives something and the rebuttal really answers it; hedges and boosters match the strength of the evidence.
A listener follows it in one hearing. No word-for-word translation from Spanish.
